record.paper_title: Mathematical open problems in Projected Entangled Pair States
record.original_question: Is the following bulk-boundary correspondence for PEPS exactly true: the parent Hamiltonian of a projected entangled pair state is gapped if and only if the corresponding boundary states can be written as Gibbs states of one-dimensional short-range Hamiltonians whose interaction terms decay exponentially with distance?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 1 The gap of the parent Hamiltonian of a PEPS corresponds exactly to the possibility of writing the boundary states as Gibbs states of 1D short range Hamiltonians

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. A Projected Entangled Pair State (PEPS) on a finite region $\Lambda \subset \mathbb{Z}^2$ is the quantum state obtained by placing, on every edge of $\Lambda$, a maximally entangled pair of $D$-dimensional virtual particles, and then applying at each vertex $v$ a linear map $A_v : (\mathbb{C}^D)^{\otimes 4} \to \mathbb{C}^d$ that contracts the four virtual indices meeting at $v$ into a single physical $d$-level system. The resulting many-body state $|\Psi_\Lambda\rangle$ on the physical Hilbert space $(\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes |\Lambda|}$ is, under standard injectivity assumptions, the unique ground state of a local frustration-free "parent Hamiltonian" $H_\Lambda = \sum_R h_R$, whose terms $h_R \ge 0$ are supported on small plaquettes.

For a region $R \subset \Lambda$ with complement $R^c$, the reduced density matrix of $|\Psi_\Lambda\rangle$ on the virtual indices crossing the boundary $\partial R$ defines, via the standard PEPS isometry, a positive operator $\rho^{\mathrm{bd}}_{\partial R}$ on the one-dimensional boundary Hilbert space, called the boundary state of the PEPS on $R$.

The family of parent Hamiltonians $\{H_\Lambda\}$ is said to be gapped if there exists $\gamma > 0$ such that for every sufficiently large region $\Lambda$, the spectral gap above the ground space of $H_\Lambda$ is at least $\gamma$.

The boundary states are said to admit a short-range Gibbs description with exponentially decaying interactions if there exist constants $C, \xi > 0$ such that for every region $R$ one can write
$$\rho^{\mathrm{bd}}_{\partial R} = \frac{1}{Z}\, e^{-K_{\partial R}}, \qquad K_{\partial R} = \sum_{X \subset \partial R} \Phi(X),$$
with self-adjoint local terms $\Phi(X)$ satisfying $\|\Phi(X)\| \le C\, e^{-\operatorname{diam}(X)/\xi}$.

Question. Is it true that the parent Hamiltonian family $\{H_\Lambda\}$ of an (injective) PEPS is gapped if and only if its boundary states admit a short-range Gibbs description with exponentially decaying interactions in the above sense?
artifact.status_search_result: One direction of the conjectured equivalence has been established rigorously: Kastoryano, Lucia, and Pérez-García (Comm. Math. Phys. 2019, arXiv:1709.07691) proved that an approximate factorization property of the boundary state — satisfied in particular by Gibbs states of local short-range 1D Hamiltonians — implies a constant spectral gap of the bulk parent Hamiltonian for injective and MPO-injective PEPS. The converse direction, and hence the full "if and only if" conjecture, does not appear to have been proven in full generality, so the problem appears to remain partially solved/open.

status_evidence.title: Locality at the boundary implies gap in the bulk for 2D PEPS
status_evidence.snippet: An approximate factorization condition on the boundary state... is sufficient to prove that the parent Hamiltonian of the bulk 2D PEPS has a constant gap... Gibbs states of a local, finite-range Hamiltonian satisfy such condition.
status_evidence.claim: The 'Gibbs-boundary implies gap' direction is rigorously proven for injective and MPO-injective PEPS.

status_evidence.title: Locality at the Boundary Implies Gap in the Bulk for 2D PEPS
status_evidence.snippet: Provides one of the first rigorous connections between boundary theories and dynamical properties in an interacting many body system.
status_evidence.claim: Published version confirms one direction of the conjectured bulk-boundary correspondence; the converse is not addressed.
